operation_tail.detail: The Spring 2026 Connected Nations update was published on 13 May 2026 and reports fixed broadband availability as of January 2026.
The Spring 2026 publication is an interim update and remains separate from CN2025, whose fixed-broadband basis was July 2025.
The fixed-broadband scope includes availability from fixed-line and fixed-wireless-access networks; the two routes remain identifiable.
Full-fibre take-up is reported as a separate metric from network availability and is not treated as coverage.
Ofcom reports full fibre available to 24.9 million UK residential premises at the January 2026 snapshot.
The reported 24.9 million residential full-fibre premises correspond to 82% of the residential premise base.
The Spring 2026 residential coverage denominator is 30.5 million UK homes.
Full-fibre availability increased by 1.2 million homes during the six months to January 2026.
Full-fibre take-up increased by 1.8 million active connections during the same six-month period.
Ofcom reports 12.4 million full-fibre broadband connections across residential and commercial premises.
The 12.4 million active full-fibre connections correspond to 47% of all premises with full-fibre coverage.
Gigabit-capable broadband availability is reported at 89% of UK homes in January 2026.
The 89% gigabit-capable figure corresponds to 27.1 million homes.
The comparison baseline is July 2025 at 87%, or 26.4 million homes; the two vintages are not merged.
Ofcom estimates approximately 4,000 premises without access to affordable decent broadband after considering lower-priced satellite services.
The fixed-line or FWA service gap is separately reported as 39,000 premises unable to access decent broadband.
The 39,000 fixed/FWA gap is compared with 44,000 premises in July 2025.
Lower-priced Starlink plans affect the affordable-decent estimate but do not rewrite fixed-line or FWA availability.
Gigabit and full-fibre coverage focus on residential properties, while take-up and decent-broadband gaps cover residential and commercial premises.
Approximately 7,000 commercial premises were not included in the affordable-USO estimate because existing connectivity such as leased lines may already be present.
The interactive report includes latest and historical observations; snapshot dates remain explicit when comparing them.
Ofcom states that data collected for Spring 2026 was used to update its broadband and mobile coverage checkers.
Royal Mail maintains the UK postcode system as a postal-delivery reference; postcode identity is not a cadastral boundary.
The outward component of a UK postcode contains two to four alphanumeric characters.
The inward component contains exactly three characters.
Postcodes form a four-level hierarchy of postcode area, district, sector and unit postcode.
The unit postcode is the base unit of postal geography.
ONS listed 124 postcode areas as August 2022 context; this historical count is not substituted for current file topology.
ONS listed 3,118 postcode districts in its August 2022 structural context.
ONS listed 12,463 postcode sectors in its August 2022 structural context.
The approximately 1.79 million live unit-postcode figure is retained only as August 2022 context.
Approximately 1.7 million live small-user postcodes were reported for August 2022.
Approximately 0.09 million live large-user postcodes were reported for August 2022.
A large-user postcode is allocated to a single address receiving at least 500 mail items per day.
A small-user postcode generally represents a collection of adjacent addresses rather than one property.
A small-user postcode may contain up to 100 addresses, while about 15 is described as more typical.
A large building with many delivery points may contain more than one unit postcode.
Postcode boundaries commonly fail to align with wards and other administrative boundaries.
ONS postcode directories allocate a postcode by matching its centroid grid reference to digital administrative boundaries.
Where a postcode straddles a boundary, some addresses and data may inevitably be assigned to the other area.
ONS notes that moving from postcode-based to address-based grid references should reduce cross-boundary allocation problems.
Postcode geography changes continuously as new addresses are created.
A single address may acquire a large-user postcode when its mail volume increases.
Operational changes may be required to keep the number of addresses in a unit postcode below 100.
Postcode areas can be recoded, so stable identity must rely on dated source records rather than text alone.
ONS warns that a postcode can be reused in a different location after only two years.
Continuous monitoring of postcode lifecycle and location is required to reduce geographic misallocation.
NSPL is intended for producers allocating postcode-level National Statistics to higher geographies.
NSPL first allocates UK postcodes to Output Areas using the same postcode-to-OA method as ONSPD.
NSPL then links Output Areas to higher geographies through a Census-population best-fit method.
NSPL higher-geography allocation differs from ONSPD point-in-polygon assignment and remains a separate semantic route.
ONSPD is a Gridlink-branded product combining Royal Mail, Ordnance Survey, National Records of Scotland, LPS Northern Ireland and ONS inputs.
ONSPD links both current and terminated UK postcodes to geography fields.
ONSPD assigns postcode points to administrative, health and other areas using point-in-polygon methodology.
When addresses in a postcode straddle a boundary, ONSPD assigns the postcode using the mean grid reference of its addresses.
ONSPD and NSPL are published with grid references at one-metre resolution across the UK.
ONS postcode products are released quarterly and are available free from the Open Geography portal.
The TXT representation uses fixed record length without text qualifiers.
The CSV representation uses variable-length comma-delimited records, double-quoted fields and field headings.
ONS includes a user guide with postcode products to document fields, methods and changes.
